title: Claude Fable, Claude Tag, and Anthropic's Culture — Cat Wu & Thariq Shihipar ft Simon Willison
summary:
This fireside chat explores the evolution of coding agents at Anthropic, focusing on Claude Code and the newly launched Claude Tag. Simon Willison moderates the conversation with Cat Wu (Head of Product, Claude Code) and Thariq Shihipar (Engineer, Claude Code). The speakers trace how Claude Code has shifted developer workflows from closely monitoring permission prompts to delegating implementation, freeing time for creative and product-level thinking. Cat highlights the shift from months-long PRD processes to rapid prototyping, while Thariq provocatively argues rewrites are now beneficial with good test suites.

Claude Tag introduces multiplayer, proactive agentic workflows in Slack, monitoring bug reports, drafting PRs, retaining team memory, and landing 65% of product engineering PRs at Anthropic. Non-engineers use it as a company search engine. The team describes fluid multiplayer workflows across design, engineering, and Claude Tag.

The team discusses their dogfooding culture, with internal bars for active users and retention before public release. Remote control—connecting to local CLI sessions via mobile—was a surprise hit. Code review is evolving toward automation, with Claude Code reviewing outer-layer changes after a six-plus-month trust-building process.

On system prompts, the team reduced Claude Code's prompt by 80% for frontier models like Fable and Opus 4.8, finding that over-constraining with examples and hard rules limited creativity. They now favor context over constraints, with different prompts per model—older models retain the full prompt.

Auto Mode is the recommended way to run long-running work safely. The team has commissioned red-teamers, built thousands of evals, and mitigated every attack found. A Sonnet classifier judges each tool call against conversation context, handling dynamic permissions and sandboxing. Beyond Auto Mode, Anthropic supports credential injection via proxy—credentials are usable by the agent but not accessible by it—and trusted devices for remote control users.

On the human element, the team encourages developers to be more ambitious and stop negotiating against themselves. Thariq challenges that perceived trade-offs should prove themselves real rather than be assumed. Simon reflects on how this upends 25 years of software intuition where the default answer was no. Thariq shares his absurd project: a 2D Street Fighter fighting game featuring himself and friends, using Claude Code to prompt Gemini and video models for sprite animations, frame verification, and JSON hitbox generation. Cat describes a rock climbing app built with Claude Code workflows that researches climbing destinations, finds direct flights, filters climbs by grade, locates Airbnbs, and prioritizes short walking approaches—what Simon dubs vibe coding Jira for mountain climbing.

In audience Q&A, Cat notes that eval tooling is less a constraint than the skill set of building great evals, and hopes to share best practices externally. On memory design, Thariq explains Claude Tag uses channel-specific shared memory stored as a markdown file per channel, with sessions contributing back to main memory, acknowledging memory research remains ongoing and unintuitive.

sections.title: Introductions and Workflow Evolution
sections.summary: Simon introduces the fireside chat with Cat Wu and Thariq Shihipar. Fable comes back online during the talk. Cat and Thariq describe how Claude Code has shifted daily work from closely monitoring permission prompts to delegating implementation, freeing time for creative and product-level thinking. Thariq notes output quality now demands higher ambition.

sections.title: Rethinking Software Engineering Norms
sections.summary: Cat describes the shift from months-long PRD and spec processes to rapid prototyping, arguing engineers need stronger product and business sense. Thariq provocatively claims rewrites are now beneficial, arguing a codebase serves as a spec. Simon adds that prototyping has become easier, even from a phone.

sections.title: Introducing Claude Tag
sections.summary: Cat and Thariq introduce Claude Tag as a multiplayer, proactive agent in Slack. It monitors bug reports, drafts PRs, retains team memory, and lands 65% of product engineering PRs at Anthropic. Claude Code remains best for complex interactive iteration, while Claude Tag handles proactive background work.

sections.title: Non-Engineer Use Cases for Claude Tag
sections.summary: Thariq describes non-engineers using Claude Tag as a company search engine, for metrics queries, and to understand features by cloning codebases. The team notes they are still early in discovering use cases.

sections.title: Multiplayer Sessions and Dogfooding
sections.summary: The team describes fluid multiplayer workflows where design, engineering, and Claude Tag collaborate on shared sessions. Social dynamics are still being ironed out. The segment touches on using Claude Code to build Claude Code, illustrating Anthropic's dogfooding culture.

sections.title: Prioritization and Dogfooding Culture
sections.summary: Cat explains the prioritization approach: heavy dogfooding internally, sharing products with Anthropic employees and early customers for brutal feedback, and maintaining a clear internal bar for active users and retention before public release. Engineers know what metrics to hit, and unpolished features cause churn.

sections.title: Surprise Success of Remote Control
sections.summary: Cat shares that remote control, allowing mobile or web browser connection to local CLI sessions, was a surprise hit. Users plug laptops into chargers, close screens, and control Claude Code from their phones. Cat initially didn't understand the need but now does it personally.

sections.title: Evolving Code Review Processes
sections.summary: Thariq describes code review varying by task: code owners for critical areas, git review on every PR, and Claude Code increasingly reviewing outer-layer changes independently. This six-plus-month trust-building process includes incident reviews feeding back into eval sets.

sections.title: Building Trust in New Model Generations
sections.summary: The team maintains eval suites ensuring new models are drop-in replacements — Fable must be strictly better than Opus 4.8. They have team-specific and Anthropic-wide evals, plus external red-teaming for auto mode against prompt injection and malicious inputs. Behavioral evals address UX issues like Claude stopping work prematurely.

sections.title: Reducing System Prompts for Frontier Models
sections.summary: The system prompt was reduced by 80% for Fable and Opus 4.8. The team found over-constraining Claude with examples and hard constraints limited creativity — removing examples helped. They now favor context over constraints, fewer instructions overall, and different system prompts per model.

sections.title: System Prompt Nuances and Per-Model Prompts
sections.summary: The team explains softening instructions like 'always verify' to acknowledge 90%/10% edge cases, relying on frontier model judgment. Only the most frontier models get the 80% token decrease; older models retain the full system prompt. Simon notes this relies on judgment that older models lacked. The team acknowledges cheaper models may not benefit from reduced prompts.

sections.title: Models Prompting Models and Prompt Transparency
sections.summary: Simon observes models are now excellent at writing prompts, using sub-agents and workflows where Claude prompts other Claude instances. He requests Anthropic publish Claude Code's tool and system prompts publicly, as they serve as documentation — he currently intercepts them via proxy and diffs old vs. new versions to learn capabilities. Cat commits to making a detailed post.

sections.title: Philosophy of Tool Design
sections.summary: The team trends toward fewer tools with distinct, easily distinguishable functions. Thariq describes tool design as more art or biology than science. The file edit tool exists primarily for deterministic UI rendering of approval prompts, but could be removed for auto mode users. The 'ask user question' tool was hard to eval and driven by dogfooding preference.

sections.title: Auto Mode and Safety
sections.summary: Almost everyone at Anthropic uses Auto Mode for safe long-running work. The team commissioned red-teamers to create adversarial environments and mitigated every attack found, with risks far lower than an average human reviewer. A Sonnet classifier judges each tool call against conversation context, handling dynamic permissions and sandboxing. Auto Mode has been used internally since January and evals will be published in coming weeks.

sections.title: Security Beyond Auto Mode and Credential Injection
sections.summary: Auto Mode is what makes Claude Tag work safely in Slack, where many users can influence the agent. The team uses a Swiss cheese defense approach with RL and other layers. Beyond Auto Mode, they support credential provisioning so Claude can act as its own identity, trusted devices for remote control users, and credential injection via proxy — agents can use credentials without accessing them, with tokens inserted on the fly.

sections.title: The Human Element and Developer Ambition
sections.summary: Simon asks about the sense of loss as models subsume traditional engineering roles. Thariq argues the offset is being more ambitious — citing colleagues who hand-wrote Zig compilers and now rewrite Bun in Rust. Cat notes the co-founders' mantra: don't negotiate against yourselves. The team sees success as fun and encourages tackling previously impossible projects.

sections.title: Evolving PM Role in an AI-Native Team
sections.summary: Cat describes the PM role changing every month — PMs are a mix of engineer, designer, and PM. They plug gaps: building prototypes to inspire engineers, doing first-pass designs, automating launch calendars and status updates, and ensuring internal announcements are detailed.

sections.title: Surprising Use Cases: AI Video Editing
sections.summary: Thariq describes using Fable to edit a conference talk video from raw files in a one-shot prompt. Fable transcribed the video, detected a popup in the deck recording, substituted HTML source, dynamically tracked and cropped Thariq as he paced the stage, and added animations using ffmpeg and remotion.

sections.title: Limitations and Future Design Aspirations
sections.summary: Thariq wants better design and UX taste from models — padding is off, interfaces aren't delightful, and models lean on existing app conventions rather than novel frontier AI interactions. He looks forward to models as interaction design thought partners and hopes for real-world interaction like orchestrating science experiments.

sections.title: Cultural Hacks for Productivity
sections.summary: Cat shares that Claude Tag works best when Slack channels are public, enabling comprehensive context search for highest accuracy. Thariq reemphasizes the co-founders' philosophy of not negotiating against yourselves — being maximally ambitious. These cultural traits help Anthropic be productive with AI tools.

sections.title: Absurd Projects, Audience Q&A, and Closing
sections.summary: Thariq challenges developers to make trade-offs prove themselves real rather than assuming them. Simon reflects on how this upends 25 years of software intuition where the default was no. For absurd projects, Thariq shares a 2D Street Fighter fighting game featuring himself and friends, built with Claude Code prompting Gemini and video models for sprite animations, frame verification, and JSON hitbox generation. Cat describes a rock climbing app using Claude Code workflows that researches destinations, finds direct flights, filters climbs by grade, locates Airbnbs, and prioritizes short walking approaches — Simon dubs it vibe coding Jira for mountain climbing. In audience Q&A, Cat says eval tooling is less the constraint than the skill set of building great evals, and plans to share best practices. On memory, Thariq explains Claude Tag uses channel-specific shared memory stored as a markdown file per channel, with sessions contributing back to main memory, noting memory research remains ongoing.
